title: Two names on one stone
hookLine: the Christian hope is that love is stronger than death
carry: not even death separates us from God's love

lines: A BLANK SPACE AFTER THE DASH.
cards: A gravestone with two names carved on it. One has both dates filled in. The other has the first date, and a blank space after the dash, waiting.
Somebody chose that stone. They stood in an office and decided their name would go next to the person they loved, while they're still alive. It's a strange, stubborn thing to do.
It says: death has taken one of us, and still hasn't separated us. The Bible has a few lines on that.

teach.b: Start with a love song. Near the end of the Song of Songs, the beloved says, in the King James words: "Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death." Not stronger.
As strong. Even that is daring: death is hard to argue with, and a love poem calls it an even match.
Then: "Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it."

Later in Romans 8, the groaning Spirit's chapter, Paul lists everything that could cut people off from God's love, and he puts death first: "For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord."

Neither death. That's where the Christian hope steps past the love song, from as strong to stronger. The reason Christians give is Easter: the belief that Jesus died and rose, so death didn't have the last say over love.

teach.h: O DEATH, WHERE IS THY STING?
teach.b: Elsewhere Paul taunts death: "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" Churches describe what that hope means for those who have died in different ways, and much of it they leave with God.
Love doesn't make death painless. The stone still has a name on it. The hope is that death doesn't get to separate what love has joined to God.

how: Christians read Romans 8:38–39 and 1 Corinthians 15 at funerals and on Easter, and the Song of Songs' line about love and death is sometimes read at weddings; some churches also remember the dead by name in their prayers.

o: the idea that a strong love keeps a person from grieving
a promise that the people we love never really die at all
the hope that not even death separates us from God's love

games.q: love is stronger — tap the pairs.
p: shall separate us from the love of God

s: the Song of Songs says love is stronger than death
it says love is "strong as death", as strong. the Christian hope of stronger leans on Romans 8 and Easter.
Paul's list of things that cannot separate us from God's love begins with death
the Christian hope says death doesn't hurt
the hope is that death can't separate us from the love of God, not that loss is painless.

games.q: you're Paul, listing everything that might cut people off from God's love: death, life, angels, powers, things present, things to come, height, depth. how does your list end?
o: nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us.
games.why: "nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." the list leaves nothing out.

practice: Bring to mind someone you love who is still here, and, if there is one, someone you love who has died, and hold them side by side for a moment, like two names on one stone.
If you pray, you can thank God for each of them by name; if you don't, let the love for both simply be there.
If grief feels too heavy to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
